''Trifolium indicum'' L. }} [[File:Melilotus indicus MHNT.BOT.2011.3.80.jpg|thumb|''Melilotus indicus'' - [[MHNT]]]][[File:Melilotus indicus flowers.jpg|thumb|Close up view of ''M. indicus'' flowers]][[File:Melilotus indicus infected with powdery mildew.jpg|thumb|Foliar powdery mildew infection ]]'''''Melilotus indicus''''', sometimes incorrectly written ''Melilotus indica'', is a yellow-flowered herb in the [[Fabaceae]] family. It is native to northern Africa, Europe and Asia, but naturalized throughout much of the rest of the world's temperate climate zones. It is a commonly occurring weed in disturbed habitats, with historical uses for forage and medicine. Common names in English include '''sweet clover''' (or '''sweet-clover'''), '''sour clover''' ('''sour-clover''', '''sourclover'''), '''Indian sweet-clover''', '''annual yellow sweetclover''', '''Bokhara clover''', '''small-flowered sweet clover''', '''common melilot''', '''small-flowered melilot''', '''small melilot''', '''sweet melilot''', '''Californian lucerne''' and '''Hexham scent'''. In [[Australia]] and [[New Zealand]], where it is naturalized, it is sometimes called '''King Island melilot''' or '''King Island clover'''.{{GRIN | name = ''Melilotus indicus'' | id = 24000}}{{cite web | title = ''Melilotus'' | work = Multilingual Multiscript Plant Name Database | url = http://www.plantnames.unimelb.edu.au/Sorting/Melilotus.html | publisher = University of Melbourne | access-date = 2009-01-04}}{{cite web |url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/cgi-bin/apni?TAXON_NAME=Melilotus+indicus |title=''Melilotus indicus'' |access-date=7 December 2012 |work=[[Australian Plant Name Index]] (APNI), IBIS database |publisher=Centre for Plant Biodiversity Research, Australian Government, Canberra |archive-date=5 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230405110005/https://www.anbg.gov.au/cgi-bin/apni?TAXON_NAME=Melilotus+indicus |url-status=dead }} ==Description== ''M. indicus'' is an [[Annual plant|annual]] herb from {{convert|10|to|50|cm|in|abbr=off}} in height (rarely to one meter), with compound leaves of trifoliate leaflets. Leaf edges are sharply dentate. The leaves have a sweet, cloying scent when crushed. The small yellow flowers are 2–3 mm and are borne in dense racemes.{{FloraBase| name = ''Melilotus indicus'' (L.) All. | id = 4085}} The flowers produce a hairless pod of similar length.Webb, D.A., Parnell, J. and Doogue, D. 1996. ''An Irish Flora.'' Dundalgan Press Ltd., Dundalk. {{ISBN|0-85221-131-7}} While similar in overall appearance to ''[[Melilotus officinalis]]'', ''M. indicus'' is typically smaller in both stem height and flower size. ==Taxonomy== It was first published as ''Trifolium indicum'' by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his 1753 ''[[Species plantarum]]''. It was transferred into ''[[Melilotus]]'' by [[Carlo Allioni]] in 1785.{{APNI | name = ''Melilotus indicus'' (L.) All. | id = 61411}} ==Distribution and habitat== It has a wide native distribution, ranging from [[Macaronesia]] and northern [[Africa]], through [[Europe]], and into temperate and tropical [[Asia]]. It is naturalized throughout most of the rest of the world, including the [[United Kingdom]], the [[United States]], [[South America]], [[Australia]] and [[New Zealand]]. In its introduced regions, it is frequently found along fields, roadsides, and other disturbed areas, and is typically considered a weed.{{Cite web |title=Mid-Atlantic Herbaria - Melilotus indicus |url=https://midatlanticherbaria.org/portal/taxa/index.php?tid=2498&taxauthid=1&clid=99 |access-date=2026-02-09 |website=midatlanticherbaria.org}} ''Melilotus indicus'' has been identified as [[halophyte]], maintaining high germination and growth rates in saline substrates.{{Cite journal |last=Rogers |first=M. All., a salt-tolerant wild leguminous herb with high potential for use as a forage crop in salt-affected soils |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0367253009000358 |journal=Flora - Morphology, Distribution, Functional Ecology of Plants |volume=204 |issue=10 |pages=737–746 |doi=10.1016/j.flora.2008.10.004 |issn=0367-2530|url-access=subscription }} == Ecology == ''[[Melilotus]]'' species are typically insect pollinated, but specific species have not been observed for ''M. indicus''.{{Cite journal |date=1999-12-01 |title=Insect pollination of cultivated crop plants |url=https://doi.org/10.5860/choice.37-2165 |journal=Choice Reviews Online |volume=37 |issue=04 |pages=37–2165-37-2165 |doi=10.5860/choice.37-2165 |issn=0009-4978|url-access=subscription }} In its introduced regions in the United States, it is often considered a weed, but is not as [[Invasive species|invasive]] as its close relative [[Melilotus officinalis|''Melilotus'' ''officinalis'']], which more aggressively outcompetes native prairie species. ''M. indicus'' can be infected by the powdery mildew species ''Erysiphe trifoliorum'', which also infects plants in the ''[[Lathyrus]]'', ''[[Medicago]],'' [[Clover|''Trifolium'']], and ''[[Vicia]]'' genera.{{Cite web |title=First Report of Erysiphe trifoliorum Causing Powdery Mildew of Melilotus indicus in Mexico |url=https://apsjournals.apsnet.org/action/cookieAbsent |access-date=2026-02-26 |website=APS Journals |language=en |doi=10.1094/PDIS-05-16-0619-PDN}} ==Uses and economic importance== ''Melilotus indicus'' is used as a source of nectar for bees, as forage{{Cite journal |last=Stevenson |first=George A. |date=1969-01-01 |title=AN AGRONOMIC AND TAXONOMIC REVIEW OF THE GENUS MELILOTUS MILL. |url=https://doi.org/10.4141/cjps69-001 |journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Science |volume=49 |issue=1 |pages=1–20 |doi=10.4141/cjps69-001 |issn=0008-4220|url-access=subscription }}, and as a soil improver through its nitrogen fixing properties. As a salt tolerant species, it is a particularly useful forage crop where other legumes cannot grow. By 1907, it was in use at [[King_Island_(Tasmania)|King Island]] for cattle fodder, explaining its Australian name.{{cite news |date=8 March 1907 |title=Melilotus |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article196782070 |newspaper=[[The Port Augusta Dispatch, Newcastle And Flinders Chronicle]] |page=4 |via=National Library of Australia}} ''Melilotus indicus'' has been used as a traditional medicine for its [[analgesic]], [[antioxidant]], [[aperitive]], [[emollient]], and anti-inflammatory properties.{{Cite journal |last=Marzouk |first=Mona |date=2021-08-08 |title=A comparative review on phytochemical constituents and biological effects of Melilotus indicus (L.)
